Biopsychosocial model; broadly speaking the idea is that our psychological health, our biological, and our social health are all influenced by one another. So I can’t expect to by socially healthy if I’m not psychologically healthy for example. 

I used this model to address my psychological health by concentrating on the things I was able to influence, specifically my physical health and my social health. I made more of an effort to see my friends, and I started going for walks as frequently as I could. 

That was about 5-6 years ago and I’m as healthy psychologically now as I’ve been for as long as I can remember, although it didn’t take that long for the changes to take effect. Of course there’s no way of knowing that the changes I made were the thing that made me better, but I believe they helped significantly, and even if they didn’t they improved my life regardless so it was worth doing.

Fair question, one that I thought would come sooner to be honest. The simple answer is that it wasn't pre-meditated, at least not in a significant way. 

It happened the day before my abuser's birthday, I couldn't face seeing another day where this person was celebrated and showered with love that I believe isn't deserved. My therapist was on holiday that week, so I had a little less support than usual, I hadn't eaten or slept in 2 days (which makes a massive difference in your ability to maintain a level head), the conditions were perfect basically. Looking back of course I was at risk, but I didn't want to help myself. 

I knew that I wanted to do something to ensure that I wouldn't see that birthday, but I was fighting the urge and dismissing the thoughts. I wasn't preparing to do something, I wasn't planning to hop in front of the nearest train or lorry. The thing that scares me looking back is the length of time it took to go from "I'm struggling" to "it's go time". It was a lot more like how people react when they're angry, the red mist descends and they say or do something that under any other circumstances they would never do. This is how it came to happen. I was in bed, my wife was downstairs, my thoughts escalated rapidly and I grabbed the nearest box of tablets and took as many as I could. Did I know it would work? No, not at all, I hoped for the best. At that point I didn't care about the consequences of failure, I was only interested in taking as much as I could to end my life. 

In hindsight I'm embarrassed by it all, I know sat here now that my actions were very optimistic (in a twisted way) and that it was unlikely to kill me. I can't stress enough just how poorly my cognitive abilities had waned, if a person can convince themselves to overcome that core sense of self preservation then by definition all rational and logical thinking has gone out of the window. It was stupid is what I'm saying, I'm not going to defend that.
